slides.0.title: Winemaking and Style
slides.0.subtitle: How winemaking choices shape style
slides.1.title: Northern Rhône reds: Syrah winemaking choices
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Whole cluster vs destemmed
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Côte-Rôtie may be fermented whole-bunch or destemmed (WineWithSeth). General account: whole bunches add stem tannin, spice and a tighter texture, destemming gives rounder, more direct fruit; this is a style choice, not a rule
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Viognier co-fermentation
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Viognier may make up to 20% of the vines in Syrah plots and the two must be vinified together from blended grapes (INAO / WineWithSeth). Over 10% is rare, interplanting is more common on the Côte Blonde. General account: adds floral lift and helps stabilise colour
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Vessels and ageing
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Fermentation may be in stainless steel, concrete, amphora or large wooden foudres; most growers age in barriques for 12–48 months; oak chips are banned (WineWithSeth)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: A stylistic spectrum
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Traditional approaches (whole bunch, old large wood, longer maceration) coexist with modern ones (destemmed, more new oak); general account: Côte-Rôtie leans aromatic and silky, Hermitage and Cornas leaner towards structure and ageing potential
slides.1.content: In tasting notes, infer winemaking from traces of whole bunch, destemming and oak, then link to style; do not rely on brand impressions.
slides.2.title: Southern Rhône reds: Grenache and GSM blends
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Grenache's oxidative tendency
slides.2.highlights.0.content: General account: Grenache has thin skins and low colour and tannin, so wines are paler and oxidise easily (brick tones and developed notes appear early); it is therefore often blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre for colour and structure and needs careful oxygen management
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Concrete, large wood and new barriques
slides.2.highlights.1.content: General account: concrete and large wood (foudre, demi-muid) preserve Grenache fruit and texture, whereas new small barriques can mask its character; practice varies by estate
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Roles in a GSM blend
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Grenache: body, alcohol, red berries and sweet spice; Syrah: colour, dark fruit, pepper and frame; Mourvèdre: tannin, meatiness and structure, late-ripening and needing a warm, long season (general account)
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape specifications
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Hand harvest and sorting are compulsory; 18 entries (13 varieties); 35 hl/ha; minimum natural alcohol 12.5% (INAO). High alcohol is the norm and a frequent exam style point
slides.2.highlights.4.title: The logic of blending
slides.2.highlights.4.content: Varieties with different ripening times and resilience complement each other and spread vintage risk; southern crus are built on Grenache with minimums (for example Gigondas and Vacqueyras at least 50%)
slides.2.content: Essay skeleton: Grenache's strengths (ripeness, fruit, drought tolerance) and weaknesses (pale colour, oxidation, high alcohol) → how blending and vessel choice compensate.
slides.3.title: White and rosé wines
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Condrieu: 100% Viognier
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Minimum natural alcohol 11.5% (INAO). Viognier is low in acid and high in alcohol, so balancing ripeness and freshness is central; oak and lees stirring vary by estate (general account)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Marsanne / Roussanne whites
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Used in Hermitage, Saint-Joseph, Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Péray. General account: Marsanne is rounder and lower in acid, Roussanne tighter in acid and aroma; often barrel-fermented and aged on lees, with MLF depending on style
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Côtes du Rhône whites
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Built on Grenache blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Viognier and others; general account: cool fermentation in stainless steel is common to keep freshness, often blocking MLF
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Tavel and Lirac rosé
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Tavel makes only rosé (Grenache noir must be in the blend), deeper in colour and fuller in body; rosé colour is usually obtained by short skin contact or direct pressing (general account)
slides.3.content: White-wine questions often combine variety (Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne, Grenache blanc) × oak × MLF × acidity, linked to style and price.
slides.4.title: Fortified, sweet and sparkling wines
slides.4.highlights.0.title: VDN: mutage fortification
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Neutral spirit of at least 96% vol. is added at 5–10% of the must volume to stop fermentation and keep natural sugar; Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise uses Muscat à petits grains, Rasteau VDN is mainly Grenache with must sugar ≥252 g/L
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Reductive vs oxidative ageing
slides.4.highlights.1.content: General account: the grenat style keeps fresh red fruit while tuilé/ambré styles age oxidatively towards dried fruit, nuts and caramel; residual sugar and minimum ageing periods differ between sources and are not examined
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Hermitage vin de paille
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Grapes must dry for at least 45 days and exceed 350 g/L sugar at pressing; a tiny-volume, very sweet speciality (INAO)
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Clairette de Die
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Ancestrale (Muscat ≥75%) finishes a single fermentation in bottle with at least 4 months' ageing; the second-fermentation version uses Clairette only and at least 9 months (INAO). Crémant de Die is the 1993 sparkling AOC
slides.4.content: Small-volume specialities are common Diploma identification questions: decide first whether it is fortified, dried or single-fermentation, then work back to sweetness and style.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the Côte-Rôtie rule on Viognier and Syrah?
A. Viognier must be added to Syrah after fermentation
B. Viognier may be up to 20% of vines in Syrah plots and is vinified together from blended grapes
C. Viognier must be at least 50%
D. Viognier is forbidden
Viognier is capped at 20% (Syrah at least 80%) and vinified together with Syrah; over 10% is rare in practice.
Neutral spirit in a VDN such as Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is added at about what share of the must volume?
5–10% (at least 96% vol.), which stops fermentation and keeps natural sugar.
Why is Grenache so often blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre?
A. Grenache is low in colour and tannin and oxidises easily, so colour and structure are added
B. Grenache is too high in acid
C. Single-variety wines are banned by law
D. Grenache ripens too late to harvest
Grenache has thin skins, pale colour, oxidation risk and high alcohol; Syrah and Mourvèdre add colour, tannin and structure (general account).
What characterises the ancestrale method of Clairette de Die?
A. Second fermentation in large stainless-steel tanks
B. A single fermentation finished in bottle, mainly Muscat
C. Fortified, then bottled
D. Grapes dried for 45 days
Ancestrale: Muscat ≥75%, a single fermentation finished in bottle and at least 4 months' ageing.
